notes.b: Biology is not just a list of separate chapters. Three cross-cutting themes, Health, Sustainability and Technology, link the chapters to the real world, and they are the way the exam asks you to use what you know.
points: The three cross-cutting themes are Health, Sustainability and Technology. They are not separate topics: they run through all three contextual strands (Organisation of Life; Structures and Processes of Life; Interactions of Life), and are shown in the specification’s diagram as a ring around them.
Each theme is a lens: a way of looking at any piece of biology to ask how it applies to a real issue today. The same topic can be viewed through more than one lens.
For example, genetically engineered insulin is a health issue (treating diabetes) and a technology issue (recombinant DNA, meaning DNA made by joining pieces from different sources).

The examination asks students to apply biology to issues linked to the themes, often using unfamiliar stimulus material (the new information given in a question) such as a news report, data or a case. This is why you must be able to bring knowledge from any chapter to the issue.
notes.tip: You may be asked to name the three themes and show how a named topic relates to each. There are only three themes, so do not add Ethics or Society as a fourth.

notes.b: The Health lens asks how biology explains health and disease, how disease is prevented, diagnosed and treated, and how lifestyle and environment affect health. The specification frames health as promoting health and reducing the risk of disease. The first group of examples is about infection and illness.
points: Vaccination and immunity: vaccinating enough people protects those who are not immune, because the disease cannot spread easily through a mostly protected population.
Emerging infectious diseases (new or newly spreading diseases): how they spread, and the reproduction number, R₀, which is the average number of people one infected person passes the disease on to.
Cancer: its causes, prevention and treatment, for example avoiding smoking and excess UV light, which both damage cells and raise cancer risk.
Vaccination against the human papillomavirus (HPV), which causes most cervical cancers, is a prevention example. It protects against HPV but you should not claim it prevents all cervical cancer.

The gut microbiome (the community of microorganisms living in the digestive tract) has a role in digestion, immunity and metabolic health. There is more on this in “Acquired immunity, prevention and treatment”, “Emergence and spread of infectious disease”, “Causes, prevention and treatment of cancer” and “The microbiome”.
notes.tip: Do not claim HPV vaccination prevents all cervical cancer: say it protects against the virus that causes most of them.

notes.h: Health: diet, the body and treatment
notes.b: The second group of Health examples covers how lifestyle, the body’s chemical signals and medical care affect health. Each is taught in its own chapter, so here you only need to know that it belongs under this lens.
points: Diet: a balanced diet supports health, while diet-related conditions include obesity and vitamin deficiencies (too little of a vitamin the body needs).
Dopamine, endorphins, exercise and addiction: these chemical signals link behaviour to mood and reward, so they connect lifestyle choices to health.
Prenatal and postnatal care: looking after health before birth and after birth, for the mother and the baby.
Blood groups and safe transfusion: matching blood groups between donor and recipient makes transfusion safe.

Hormonal treatments, such as insulin and the contraceptive pill, use hormones (chemical messengers in the blood) to treat or control a condition. There is more on this in “Diet”, “Vitamins”, “Dopamine and endorphins”, “Prenatal and postnatal care”, “Blood” and “Hormonal manipulation”.
notes.tip: Given a health issue in an exam, name the biology involved first, then say how it promotes health or reduces the risk of disease.

notes.b: Sustainability means meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. The Sustainability lens asks how human activity affects ecosystems, biodiversity, resources and climate, and how biology can help people live within the planet’s limits.
points: Biodiversity loss (fewer species and less variety of life) happens through habitat destruction, pollution, invasive species and climate change. Conservation is the effort to protect it.

The carbon cycle, carbon sinks (stores that take in more carbon than they release) and climate change, including Ireland’s peat bogs, which store large amounts of carbon as peat and release it as CO₂ when drained or burned.
The nitrogen cycle matters because excess fertiliser or slurry washing into rivers and lakes causes eutrophication: algal blooms that use up oxygen when they decay, killing fish.
Decomposers and soil microbiomes recycle nutrients, so nutrients are returned to the soil for plants to reuse instead of being lost.
notes.tip: Sustainability is also one of the four factors used to evaluate a scientist’s impact. Define it once, as meeting present needs without harming future generations. There is more on this in “Biodiversity loss and conservation”, “Climate change and biological strategies” and “Ethics and sustainability of nutrient cycling”.

notes.h: Sustainability: plants, enzymes and a post-fossil-fuel world
notes.b: Sustainability is not only about damage. Biology also offers ways to reduce human impact, from plants taking in carbon to enzymes that cut energy use.
points: Photosynthesis is a carbon sink, because plants take CO₂ from the air and build it into carbohydrates, removing carbon from the atmosphere.
Enzymes (biological catalysts) are used in biofuels, and in detergents that wash at lower temperatures, which saves energy.
The role of biology in a post-fossil-fuel world: using biological resources and processes to meet energy and material needs when fossil fuels are no longer burned.
notes.tip: There is more on this in “The microbiome”, “Photosynthesis as an anabolic process” and “Industrial enzymes”.

notes.b: Technology is the application of scientific knowledge to make tools, techniques and products. The Technology lens works in two directions: how technology lets biologists find out more, and how biological knowledge is used to make new technologies.
points: Biotechnology is the use of living organisms or their parts, such as enzymes, to make useful products or carry out processes.
Technologies that extend what biologists can study include light and electron microscopes, which show cells and structures too small to see by eye.
DNA sequencing and genome databases use computers to analyse huge amounts of genetic data, which would be impossible to read by hand.

Data loggers and sensors in investigations record measurements automatically, and digital tools are used for modelling and analysing data. There is more on this in “Microscopy”, “DNA sequencing” and “Bioinformatics: genome databases”.
notes.tip: Give one sentence per example and name where it is taught; you are not asked to teach the full biology of each technology in a themes answer.

notes.b: Biotechnologies are the technologies built from biological knowledge. They show the second direction of the Technology lens, and each is taught in detail elsewhere.
points: Genetic engineering, for example human insulin made by bacteria, so that insulin can be produced in large amounts.
PCR and DNA profiling are used in forensics (solving crimes) and paternity testing (finding a child’s father).
Immobilised enzymes (enzymes fixed in place) and bioreactors (vessels in which living cells or enzymes make a product) are used in industry.
Microorganisms are used in pharmaceutical, agricultural, medical and food industries.
Antenatal screening (tests during pregnancy) and fertility treatment are biotechnologies applied to reproduction.

Stem cells and gene technologies raise ethical questions, which are discussed in “Ethics of genetic technologies”. There is more on this in “Genetic engineering”, “DNA profiling”, “Industrial enzymes”, “Microorganisms in industry”, “Prenatal and postnatal care” and “Fertility control and infertility”.

notes.b: A new technology is never just a benefit. Evaluating one means asking what it costs and who it affects.
points: New technologies raise questions as well as benefits: cost and access (who can afford it), safety, the privacy of genetic data, and effects on the environment.
The factors for evaluating technologies and the scientists behind them are in “Science, scientists and society”.
notes.tip: In a discussion answer, give at least one benefit and one concern, such as cost, safety, privacy or environmental effect.

notes.h: Applying a lens to an issue
notes.b: In the exam you are often given an unfamiliar issue and asked to discuss it. A fixed method means you can start from the biology you know and build an answer step by step.
points: 1. Identify the biology behind the issue: the structures, processes or organisms involved.
2. Say which theme or themes it relates to, and why.
3. Explain the issue’s causes or mechanism using that biology.
4. Give its benefits or problems, with evidence, so your points are backed up by data or facts from the question.
5. Suggest actions or solutions based on the biology.
6. Note the links to the other themes, because most issues fit more than one lens.
notes.tip: Exams give stimulus material such as a disease outbreak, biodiversity loss or a new biotechnology and ask you to explain the biology and discuss it through one or more themes.

notes.b: Antibiotic resistance touches all three themes, so it shows the method at work. Follow the steps: biology first, then each lens, then actions.
points: Biology: bacteria with mutations that let them survive an antibiotic survive and reproduce, so resistant strains increase by natural selection.
Health: infections such as MRSA (an antibiotic-resistant bacterium) become hard or impossible to treat.
Sustainability: overuse of antibiotics in medicine and in farming speeds this up. Antibiotics are a resource that is being used up faster than new ones are found.
Technology: rapid diagnostic tests show whether an infection is bacterial, genome sequencing tracks resistant strains, and new antibiotics are sought.
Actions: prescribe antibiotics only for bacterial infections, take them exactly as prescribed, improve hygiene and vaccination to reduce infections, and limit antibiotic use in farm animals.
notes.tip: Always start with the biology (natural selection), then attach each theme, so every point is explained rather than just named.

notes.b: Irish peatlands are mainly a Sustainability issue with a Technology link. The method starts with why peat forms, then shows what happens when it is disturbed.
points: Biology: in waterlogged, acidic, low-oxygen bogs, decomposers work very slowly, so dead plant material, mainly Sphagnum moss, builds up as peat, storing carbon.
Sustainability: draining and cutting bogs for fuel lets oxygen in, so the peat decomposes or is burned, releasing CO₂. Bogs are also habitats for specialised species.
Action: Bord na Móna ended industrial peat harvesting in 2021, and drained bogs are being rewetted to stop carbon loss and restore habitats.
Technology: satellite and sensor monitoring of water levels and greenhouse-gas release.
Health link: burning peat and other solid fuels pollutes the air.
notes.tip: Link the biology to the issue: slow decomposition builds peat, and draining reverses that and releases CO₂.

keyTerms.definition: Health, Sustainability and Technology: lenses through which biology is applied to contemporary issues.
The lens asking how biology explains health and disease, and how disease is prevented, diagnosed and treated.
Meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
The application of scientific knowledge to make tools, techniques and products.
The use of living organisms or their parts, such as enzymes, to make useful products or carry out processes.
Excess nutrients in water causing algal blooms that use up oxygen when they decay, killing fish.
A store that takes in more carbon than it releases, such as a peat bog or photosynthesising plants.
The average number of people one infected person infects; see “Emergence and spread of infectious disease”.

questions.prompt: Name the three cross-cutting themes in Leaving Certificate Biology and give one biological example of an issue linked to each.
questions.model: The three cross-cutting themes are Health, Sustainability and Technology. Health: vaccination and immunity, since vaccinating enough people protects those who are not immune, or vaccination against HPV, which causes most cervical cancers. Sustainability: biodiversity loss through habitat destruction, pollution, invasive species and climate change, or eutrophication of rivers and lakes by excess fertiliser. Technology: DNA sequencing and genome databases, which use computers to analyse huge amounts of genetic data, or human insulin made by genetically engineered bacteria.

questions.prompt: Antibiotic resistance is described as a health, sustainability and technology issue. Explain why, using your knowledge of biology.
questions.model: The biology: bacteria with mutations that let them survive an antibiotic survive and reproduce, so resistant strains increase by natural selection. Health: infections such as MRSA become hard or impossible to treat. Sustainability: overuse of antibiotics in medicine and in farming speeds up resistance, and antibiotics are a resource being used up faster than new ones are found. Technology: rapid diagnostic tests show whether an infection is bacterial, genome sequencing tracks resistant strains, and new antibiotics are sought. Actions: prescribe antibiotics only for bacterial infections, take them exactly as prescribed, improve hygiene and vaccination to reduce infections, and limit antibiotic use in farm animals.

questions.prompt: Explain why Irish bogs are important carbon sinks and how human activity affects them.
questions.model: In waterlogged, acidic, low-oxygen bogs, decomposers work very slowly, so dead plant material, mainly Sphagnum moss, builds up as peat, which stores carbon. Human activity affects bogs when they are drained and cut for fuel. Draining lets oxygen in, so the peat decomposes or is burned, releasing CO₂ into the atmosphere, and the bogs lose the habitats of specialised species. A response is rewetting: Bord na Móna ended industrial peat harvesting in 2021, and drained bogs are being rewetted to stop carbon loss and restore habitats. Technology such as satellite and sensor monitoring of water levels and greenhouse-gas release can support this work.
